newsitem.title: USA: U.S. producer prices fall for fifth straight month.
newsitem.headline: U.S. producer prices fall for fifth straight month.

text.p: U.S. producer prices fell for the fifth straight month in May, dropping by 0.3 percent, the Labour Department said on Friday in a report that was likely to be greeted warmly on Wall Street.

It was the first time in 45 years that wholesale prices have dropped for five consecutive months. The May decline followed a whopping 0.6 percent price drop in April. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, producer prices fell by 0.3 percent last month, after a 0.1 percent drop in April.
Wall Street analysts had expected producer prices to post a small 0.1 percent gain in May.

The surprise drop in prices last month is likely to reinforce growing expecations on Wall Street that the inflation-wary Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its policy-making meeting early next month.

"I think this was a great report, and (the trend) is likely to continue," said Vincent Malanga, president of Lasalle Economics. "Over the next three months, we're probably more likely to see continued negative numbers on the PPI, and perhaps even the CPI, than positive numbers."

Stock and bond prices leaped on Thursday after the government reported that retail sales slid in May. That report fanned hopes among investors that the economy was slowing from its torrid -- and potentially inflationary -- first-quarter pace.
The bond market continued its climb after Friday's report, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond up half a point. Its yield slipped to 6.74 percent from 6.78 on Thursday.

"It's just remarkable," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "There's no question that there's very little sign of upward pressure on prices at the wholesale level; there's no sign of significant upward pressure at the consumer level, so inflation remains surprisingly very benign."

The May decline in wholesale prices was led by another steep drop in energy costs. Gasoline prices in particular fell sharply, dropping by more than 7 percent, the biggest decline in more than 2-1/2 years.
Prices of a variety of other goods also fell. Car prices tumbled more than 1.5 percent, the largest drop since October 1994. Computer prices also fell, by over 4.5 percent.

However, food prices at the wholesale level rose, with prices for beef, veal, fish and fruit all higher. Fruit prices increased by nearly 8 percent, as lemon prices soared by more than 70 percent and strawberry prices rose 28 percent.

The producer price report also showed that there is not much inflation in the pipeline. Prices of intermediate goods, which are goods used to make finished wholesale products, fell by 0.2 percent in May. But prices of crude goods, materials at the start of the production process, rose by 1.3 percent after a 0.9 percent drop in April, a development that some analysts noted with caution.
"It's possible that as the year wears on we might see some increased pressure in the pipeline," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.
